catalog_quote: [p.269] 2.2 The Stress Group Lawa Stress Group has one or two syllables. Only loanwords from Thai may have three syllables (for example: [nali'ka] 'watch'). Each Stress Group has as its nucleus one stressed syllable, which always occupies the final position in the group. As its periphery, it has one weakly stressed or unstressed syllable. Its structure is (W)S: 'paŋ 'bottle' lə'pat 'to flow' si'cai 'in a hurry' ... [p.270] (The symbol ['] is used to mark a stressed syllable, [ˌ] a weakly stressed syllable, and [ ] (no symbol) an unstressed syllable). ... [p.271] 2.3.2.1 Nuclear syllable This is stressed, and functions as the nucleus of the Stress Group, and always occupies the final position. (2) Deciding source is a 46-page dedicated phonology article (1985) on exactly this languoid's dialect (Ban Pa Pae, Mae Sariang = Western Lawa), with an explicit Stress Group statement: nucleus stressed, always final; periphery weakly stressed (minor syllable, open or closed) or unstressed (CV presyllable, /i ə u/ only); trisyllables only Thai loans, also final-stressed. Glottolog lists no fuller grammar or later phonology for west2396; the one grammar sketch (Jiranan 1985, held) agrees on p.19. sources.citation: Schlatter, Donald. 1976. Lavüa' (Lawa, Lua'). In William A. Smalley (ed.), Phonemes and orthography: Language planning in ten minority languages of Thailand (Pacific Linguistics C-43), 273-282. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-C43 (whole volume, open at sealang PL archive).
sources.quote: 'When morphemes are not monosyllabic the initial syllable is made up of an unstressed minor syllable which is almost always /sə pə kə rə lə/ except in borrowed words ... Trisyllabic words are very rare, and are usually compounds.' Also p.279: 'In two syllable words the vowel of the minor syllable /ə/ is predictable, and not written.'
sources.note: Primary source behind the held Jiranan 1985 phonology summary (La-Up dialect); states initial minor syllable is unstressed (p.278) — corroborates final stress from an independent fieldworker.

sources.citation: Mitani, Yasuyuki. 1972. Rawa-go on'in-ron no kenkyū [Studies in the Lawa Phonology]. Tōnan Ajia Kenkyū (Southeast Asian Studies) 10(2): 174-196. DOI 10.20495/tak.10.2_174 (open, J-STAGE). Japanese; three dialects: Bo Luang, Umphai, Mae Sariang.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or at Harvard
sources.quote: Sec. 1.1 defines the phonological word 'setting aside stress and tone' as (C V)(minor syllable) + main syllable; sec. 1.4: the phonemes of the minor syllable have the same values as in the main syllable 'except that the vowel is always weak and short' (母音が常に弱くかつ短い), written [ə]. No explicit stress-placement rule, but the sesquisyllabic (minor + major-final) structure matches the coding.
sources.locator: sec. 1.1 (syllable/word structure) and sec. 1.4 (minor syllable); text layer lines ~185-215, ~915-960
